units.text: INT. EARNEST - CONTINUOUS
Coming over very slowly.
But I don’t like German. It isn’t at all a becoming language. I know perfectly well that I look quite plain after my German lesson.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Child, you know how anxious your guardian is that you should improve yourself in every way. He laid particular stress on your German, as he was leaving for town yesterday. Indeed, he always lays stress on your German when he is leaving for town.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: Dear Uncle Jack is so very serious! Sometimes he is so serious that I think he cannot be quite well.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Drawing herself up.

Your guardian enjoys the best of health, and his gravity of demeanour is especially to be commended in one so comparatively young as he is. I know no one who has a higher sense of duty and responsibility.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: I suppose that is why he often looks a little bored when we three are together.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Cecily! I am surprised at you. Mr. Worthing has many troubles in his life. Idle merriment and triviality would be out of place in his conversation. You must remember his constant anxiety about that unfortunate young man his brother.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: I wish Uncle Jack would allow that unfortunate young man, his brother, to come down here sometimes. We might have a good influence over him, Miss Prism. I am sure you certainly would. You know German, and geology, and things of that kind influence a man very much.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Cecily begins to write in her diary.
Shaking her head.

I do not think that even I could produce any effect on a character that according to his own brother’s admission is irretrievably weak and vacillating. Indeed I am not sure that I would desire to reclaim him. I am not in favour of this modern mania for turning bad people into good people at a moment’s notice. As a man sows so let him reap. You must put away your diary, Cecily. I really don’t see why you should keep a diary at all.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: I keep a diary in order to enter the wonderful secrets of my life. If I didn’t write them down, I should probably forget all about them.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Memory, my dear Cecily, is the diary that we all carry about with us.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: Yes, but it usually chronicles the things that have never happened, and couldn’t possibly have happened. I believe that Memory is responsible for nearly all the three-volume novels that Mudie sends us.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Do not speak slightingly of the three-volume novel, Cecily. I wrote one myself in earlier days.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: Did you really, Miss Prism? How wonderfully clever you are! I hope it did not end happily? I don’t like novels that end happily. They depress me so much.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: The good ended happily, and the bad unhappily. That is what Fiction means.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: I suppose so. But it seems very unfair. And was your novel ever published?
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Alas! no. The manuscript unfortunately was abandoned.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: Cecily starts.
I use the word in the sense of lost or mislaid. To your work, child, these speculations are profitless.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: Smiling.
But I see dear Dr. Chasuble coming up through the garden.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Rising and advancing.
Dr. Chasuble! This is indeed a pleasure.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: Enter Canon Chasuble.
And how are we this morning? Miss Prism, you are, I trust, well?
units.name: CHASUBLE

units.text: Miss Prism has just been complaining of a slight headache. I think it would do her so much good to have a short stroll with you in the Park, Dr. Chasuble.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: Cecily, I have not mentioned anything about a headache.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: No, dear Miss Prism, I know that, but I felt instinctively that you had a headache. Indeed I was thinking about that, and not about my German lesson, when the Rector came in.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: I hope, Cecily, you are not inattentive.
units.name: CHASUBLE

units.text: Oh, I am afraid I am.
units.name: CECILY

units.text: That is strange. Were I fortunate enough to be Miss Prism’s pupil, I would hang upon her lips.
units.name: CHASUBLE

units.text: Miss Prism glares.
I spoke metaphorically.—My metaphor was drawn from bees. Ahem! Mr. Worthing, I suppose, has not returned from town yet?
units.name: CHASUBLE

units.text: We do not expect him till Monday afternoon.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: Ah yes, he usually likes to spend his Sunday in London. He is not one of those whose sole aim is enjoyment, as, by all accounts, that unfortunate young man his brother seems to be. But I must not disturb Egeria and her pupil any longer.
units.name: CHASUBLE

units.text: Egeria? My name is Lætitia, Doctor.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: Bowing.
A classical allusion merely, drawn from the Pagan authors. I shall see you both no doubt at Evensong?
units.name: CHASUBLE

units.text: I think, dear Doctor, I will have a stroll with you. I find I have a headache after all, and a walk might do it good.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: With pleasure, Miss Prism, with pleasure. We might go as far as the schools and back.
units.name: CHASUBLE

units.text: That would be delightful. Cecily, you will read your Political Economy in my absence. The chapter on the Fall of the Rupee you may omit. It is somewhat too sensational. Even these metallic problems have their melodramatic side.
units.name: MISS PRISM

units.text: Goes down the garden with Dr. Chasuble.
